item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.description: Stanford Events — Branner Earth Sciences Library & Map Collection Exhibit: Water in the West Our Fall 2026 exhibition highlights the water resources in California & the Western United States to shed light on the issues that affect our waterways. The exhibit features maps and the Layperson’s guides series published by the Water Education Foundation, which aim to foster public understanding of water resources. These resources help inform collaborative decision-making to build collective solutions for water issues across the Western United States. The exhibit is available for viewing Monday through Friday during regular library open hours. Check out past exhibits and subscribe to the Branner Library Newsletter. item.description: Stanford Events — The Stanford Energy Seminar has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. We aim to bring a wide variety of perspectives to the Stanford community – academics, entrepreneurs, utilities, non-profits, and more. About the talk Water scarcity, rising energy demand, and global emissions are major sustainability challenges of the 21st century. This talk will highlight three soft matter-enabled technologies that the Diaz-Marin lab is developing to tackle these challenges. First, he will present their multiscale design of hydrogel-salt composites to produce water from air in any geography and at costs comparable to those of tap water. item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for an afternoon of poetry on the porch, in celebration of Creative Writing lecturers Stephanie Horvath and Hieu Minh Nguyen, as they launch their newest poetry collections Field of Vision and Staying Still. This event is open to Stanford affiliates and the general public. Refreshments provided and books available for purchase. Registration is encouraged but not required; register here. ____ In Horvath's Field of Vision, we traverse the thresholds of past and future, reality and dream, as we accompany the speaker through deserts, forests, rivers, and coasts. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Jacob Kegerreis - "The destructive formation of moons and rings"
item.description: Stanford Events — How did our massive moon, Mars's tiny moons, and Saturn's icy rings form? In spite of the dramatically different planetary environments, the leading (though much debated!) explanations for all these topics involve violent collisions. Earth's Moon has played a key role in our planet's evolution as a habitable world, while ancient Mars and Saturn's ocean-rich icy moons are among the most promising places where life could survive beyond Earth. We study the competing origin scenarios for each system using high-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations. For Saturn's rings -- indicated by Cassini to be remarkably young, in conflict with most established origin ideas -- a giant impact between two precursor moons could scatter debris throughout the system to evolve into the nearly pure-ice rings and varied moons we see today. item.title: Ivetta Sergeeva — The Authoritarian Passport: How States Discipline Emigrants
item.description: Stanford Events — Citizenship is conventionally understood as a source of rights and protection. It is also a source of dependency: states retain distinctive authority over passports, legal identities, civil status, and mobility that citizens need even when they live abroad. Under authoritarianism, these dependencies become instruments of political control. The study introduces extraterritorial authoritarian citizenship, a continuing relationship in which emigrants depend on origin-state institutions whose provision of nominally universal rights is politically conditional. It generates latent leverage: the capacity to impose costs without exercising it against anyone in particular. Emigrants may curb dissent even when never targeted, and transnational repression activates leverage already at work. item.title: Book Talk with Logan Wright | Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World
item.description: Stanford Events — Economic competition between the United States and China has been a defining issue of the twenty-first century. But after years of rapid growth, China's economy has faltered. How did its long-term economic outlook change so quickly? And can Beijing change course and preserve China's political ambition for global economic primacy? Join Logan Wright, author of Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World, for a book talk exploring these questions and more co-hosted by the Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions and the Hoover History Lab. A light reception will follow the talk from 5:30-6:00 PM. This event will be recorded. ______________ About the Speakers Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads the firm’s China Markets Research work. item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for a film screening of Latvia's submission for the Academy Awards and commentary from Dr. Karla Oeler, Director of the Center for Russian, Eastern European, and Eurasian Studies and Associate Professor of Film and Media Studies in the Department of Art & Art History. Ulya (2026) is a true story about Uljana Semjonova, who is a very tall girl living on a remote farm in Soviet Latvia in 1964. Her height, almost two meters, worries her family, who aren't sure how she will fit into the world. When her class photo reaches basketball coaches, she is taken to Riga to train with TTT Riga. She works hard but feels torn, because basketball doesn't give her the ordinary life she dreams of. After running away back home, she realizes that both the village and the sport see her only as "the tall girl."
